questions.text: Describe the structure of the Election Commission of Indian.
questions.text_as_printed: Describe the structure of the Election Commission of Indian. (A)

answer.value:
Structure of the Election Commission of India:
Article 324 of the Constitution outlines the formation of the Election Commission of India.
It was established on January 25, 1950.
Initially, it consisted of only one Chief Election Commissioner.
Since 1993, it comprises one Chief Election Commissioner and two other Election Commissioners.
All three Commissioners have equal powers.
In case of disagreements, decisions are made by majority.

questions.text: Explain the following in detail RO, VVPAT, NOTA, NVD, SVEEP
questions.text_as_printed: Explain the following in detail RO, VVPAT, NOTA, NVD, SVEEP (D)

answer.value:
RO (Returning Officer): The officer appointed by the Election Commission of India to conduct and manage the election process in a constituency.
VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail): A device attached to the Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) that shows a paper slip for a few seconds, allowing the voter to verify to whom their vote has been cast.
NOTA (None of the Above): An option that allows voters to indicate that none of the contesting candidates deserve their vote.
NVD (National Voters' Day): Celebrated on January 25 every year since 2011 to mark the foundation day of the Election Commission of India.

answer.value:

In such a government, allied parties share positions in the Council of Ministers.

Since 1989, coalition governments have been formed in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies in India.

questions.text: Explain briefly about the electoral constituency.
questions.text_as_printed: Explain briefly about the electoral constituency. (D)

answer.value:
Electoral Constituency:
For election purposes, the country and states are divided into smaller electoral divisions called constituencies.
These constituencies are divided based on population.
There are two types: Lok Sabha constituencies and Vidhan Sabha constituencies.
Candidates elected from Lok Sabha constituencies are called Members of Parliament (MPs).
Candidates elected from Vidhan Sabha constituencies are called Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs).
Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as per regulations.
After the 128th Constitutional Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) becomes law, 33% of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies will be reserved for women.
These are called reserved constituencies.
